summary: Specifies the data formats and code points for the IS-IS extensions that support TRILL, a protocol providing transparent Layer 2 forwarding with encapsulation and link-state routing. It was replaced by RFC 7176.

eli5.summary: TRILL switches share maps of the network using IS-IS. This defines the exact message formats they use to do it. Replaced by RFC 7176.

subtitle: How TRILL switches discover each other and route transparently across networks.

tldr.problem: TRILL is a protocol for transparent Layer 2 forwarding across large networks, but it needed a routing protocol to let TRILL switches (RBridges) discover each other and learn the network topology.
tldr.mechanism: TRILL reuses IS-IS, an existing link-state routing protocol, by extending it with new TLV (Type-Length-Value) message fields that carry TRILL-specific information like nicknames, VLAN assignments, and tree information. IS-IS Hello messages help switches discover neighbors; IS-IS Link State PDUs advertise the topology.
tldr.outcome: TRILL switches can automatically discover all other switches on the network and compute optimal paths for frames, enabling large Layer 2 networks with loop prevention and support for multipathing. RFC 7176 later updated this standard.

today: RFC 6326 specifies the IS-IS extensions for TRILL. It was obsoleted by RFC 7176, which consolidated multiple related RFCs into a single updated specification. The core concepts of using IS-IS for TRILL topology discovery and the basic TLV and sub-TLV structures remain the same.

sections.title: TRILL and Link-State Routing
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) enables switches to forward frames transparently across large networks, solving the complexity and scalability limitations of traditional spanning tree protocols. TRILL uses encapsulation (wrapping frames in a TRILL header) and hop counts (limiting frame lifetime) to prevent loops safely, and employs link-state routing to compute optimal paths.

For link-state routing to work, TRILL switches need a protocol for discovering neighbors and sharing topology information. Rather than inventing a new protocol, TRILL leverages IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System), an established routing protocol used in many networks. IS-IS was originally designed for IPv4 routing but has been extended to support multiple network types.

This RFC, together with RFC 6165, specifies all the extensions to IS-IS needed to support TRILL. The extensions include new TLVs (Type-Length-Value message fields) for carrying TRILL-specific data like switch nicknames, VLAN mappings, and distribution tree information.
sections.eli5: TRILL switches need to gossip about what they see on the network so they can learn the best routes. IS-IS is the gossip protocol; this RFC says what TRILL-specific gossip looks like.

sections.title: IS-IS Messages and TRILL Extensions
sections.content:
IS-IS operates using two main types of messages. IIH (IS-IS Hello) PDUs are broadcast on links to discover and maintain neighbor relationships. LSP (Link State PDU) messages flood through the network, advertising topology information that each switch has learned. Both message types carry TLVs, which are tagged fields that carry different kinds of information.

For TRILL, new TLVs are added to IS-IS messages. A Group Address TLV (type 142) in LSPs advertises multicast group listeners on a switch's ports. The MT-PORT-CAP (Multi-Topology-Aware Port Capability) TLV in Hello messages carries sub-TLVs specific to each port, including the Special VLANs and Flags sub-TLV that identifies the sender's nickname, the designated VLAN for the link, and port capabilities (whether it is an access port, trunk port, appointed forwarder, etc.).

Other sub-TLVs carried in LSPs include the Nickname sub-TLV (listing nicknames the switch holds), the Trees sub-TLV (specifying how many distribution trees to compute), and the Interested VLANs sub-TLV (listing VLANs the switch serves and their multicast roots). These allow TRILL switches to agree on topology, tree construction, and VLAN handling.
sections.eli5: IS-IS Hello messages let switches say 'hi, I am switch 45 and I handle VLANs 1-100.' Link State messages say 'I know the path to switch 99.' TRILL adds extra fields to carry TRILL-specific job assignments.

sections.title: Nicknames, VLANs, and MTU Discovery
sections.content:
In TRILL, each switch holds a short numeric nickname (a 16-bit integer like 0x4567) used as a shorthand in forwarding decisions and frame headers, rather than using lengthy MAC addresses or IP addresses. Switches compete for nicknames based on a priority value advertised in the Nickname sub-TLV. A switch advertises the nicknames it holds and can hold simultaneously.

Switches also advertise which VLANs they serve using the Enabled-VLANs sub-TLV in Hello messages, which is a bitmap of VLAN IDs. The Appointed Forwarders sub-TLV designates which switch on a link is responsible for forwarding frames for each VLAN, preventing duplicate forwarding.

TRILL also supports optional MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) discovery through special MTU-probe and MTU-ack PDUs. A switch sends an MTU-probe with a specific payload size, and a receiving switch responds with an MTU-ack echoing the same size if it can handle it. This allows switches to discover the maximum frame size supported across a path before forwarding user traffic, avoiding fragmentation.
sections.eli5: TRILL switches use short nicknames like 'switch 45' instead of long addresses. They advertise which VLANs they handle and test whether all switches on a link can handle the same large frame size.

sections.title: Distribution Trees and Multicast Handling
sections.content:
TRILL uses distribution trees for multicast and unknown-unicast frames. Instead of flooding frames everywhere, all switches route them along pre-computed spanning trees rooted at specific switches. The Trees sub-TLV carries three values: how many trees to compute, the maximum number of trees the switch can support, and how many of those computed trees the switch plans to use.

The Tree Identifiers sub-TLV lists which switch (by nickname) is the root of each distribution tree. For example, tree 1 might be rooted at switch 45, and tree 2 at switch 67. Switches use this information to compute the forwarding paths for frames traveling on each tree.

The Group MAC Address sub-TLV (carried within the Group Address TLV) advertises multicast group membership on a switch's ports, specifying which MAC addresses represent listener groups, the VLAN they are on, and which source addresses are interested in them. This allows efficient multicast forwarding without requiring separate multicast protocols.
sections.eli5: Instead of flooding multicast to everyone, TRILL picks a few switches as 'tree roots' and routes multicast frames along branches from those roots. The Group MAC sub-TLV says 'I have listeners for group X on VLAN Y.'

sections.title: Protocol Registrations and Code Points
sections.content:
TRILL required two new IS-IS PDU types for MTU discovery. The MTU-PROBE-PDU (PDU type 23) is sent by a switch to test frame sizes on a link. The MTU-ACK-PDU (PDU type 28) is the response. Both carry a Probe ID (an identifier for the test), the source system ID, and optionally the responder's system ID, along with padding to reach the test size.

Eleven new sub-TLVs were registered in existing IS-IS TLV spaces: VLAN-FLAGS, Enabled-VLANs, and Appointed Forwarders under the MT-PORT-CAP TLV for Hello messages; and Nickname, Trees, Tree Identifiers, and others under the Router Capability TLV for LSPs. Each sub-TLV type has a numeric code (e.g., Nickname is sub-TLV 6 of the Router Capability TLV).

A new sub-registry was created for Group Address TLV sub-types, with the Group MAC Address sub-TLV registered as type 1. The RFC also assigned NLPID 0xC0 to TRILL so that Protocols Supported TLVs in IS-IS PDUs can identify TRILL traffic.
sections.eli5: The RFC officially registers new message types and field types so that IS-IS implementations can recognize TRILL-specific information and handle it correctly.
